name: The fake deep scan
pattern: The optimizer runs a dramatic 45-second "deep scan" with a throbbing progress bar and scrolling file names. The work it's pretending to do takes under a second — the delay is theater to make the result feel earned.
tell: The scan always takes about the same showy length no matter how fast your PC is, and nothing it "found" maps to a change you can verify.
honest_version: An honest tool shows the real elapsed time on its checks — usually a few seconds — because the truth doesn't need a costume.

name: The invented issue counter
pattern: The scan ends with a big red "847 issues found!" Most of those "issues" are harmless leftover files, cookies, and registry entries that affect nothing, counted up to look alarming.
tell: The number is huge, precise, and scary, but the app won't tell you what a single "issue" actually does or what fixing it changes.
honest_version: An honest tool names what it found and why it matters, and is comfortable saying "nothing here needs fixing" — a clean result is a real result, not a failure to sell.

name: The fake optimization score
pattern: Your PC gets a score like "61/100" with no explanation of how it's calculated. After you click the button, it jumps to "94/100" — a number designed to go up, not to mean anything.
tell: The score moves the instant you "optimize," before anything could possibly have been measured, and the formula behind it is never shown.
honest_version: An honest tool shows a real before-and-after measurement with its margin of error, and will tell you when a change made no measurable difference.

name: Scareware fear-tone
pattern: The whole interface leans on alarm — red banners, warning triangles, countdowns, "Your PC is at risk!" The fear is the product; a worried person clicks and pays faster than a calm one.
tell: Everything is framed as urgent and dangerous, and the only cure on offer is their button or their subscription.
honest_version: An honest tool uses calm, specific language and saves real warnings for real risks — a tool that's always screaming has nothing left to say when something actually matters.

name: The RAM cleaner sold as a booster
pattern: A widget shows your RAM "filling up" and a button to "free" it for more FPS. It force-empties memory Windows was using as a smart cache — so the system has to reload it moments later, often making things slightly worse.
tell: It treats used RAM as a problem, but free RAM isn't doing you any good — memory exists to be used, and Windows already manages it.
honest_version: An honest tool leaves memory management to Windows and only flags RAM when you're genuinely running out, which shows up as real stutter, not a scary-looking bar.

name: The paid driver-updater subscription
pattern: An app warns that dozens of your drivers are "outdated" and offers to fix them all for a yearly fee. It bundles generic, sometimes wrong driver versions, and the scary "outdated" count is mostly drivers that are working fine.
tell: It wants a subscription to do something the vendors do for free, and it flags drivers as urgent that have no reason to change.
honest_version: An honest tool points you to the one driver that actually matters — your graphics driver, straight from the vendor — and leaves working drivers alone.

name: The tweak mega-pack with no undo
pattern: One button applies dozens of registry, service, and system changes at once, promised as the "ultimate" setup. When something breaks afterward — audio, anti-cheat, updates — there's no way to tell which of the dozens of changes did it, and often no clean way back.
tell: It changes many things in one click and offers no per-change undo, just a vague promise that it's all safe.
honest_version: An honest tool changes one thing at a time, records exactly what it did, and gives you a one-click rollback for each change.

name: The "+40% FPS" claim with no method
pattern: A bold percentage promises huge free frames. There's no mention of what hardware, what game, how many runs, or whether the gain even clears normal run-to-run wobble — because under real measurement it usually vanishes.
tell: A big percentage with no test conditions and no margin of error attached is a marketing number, not a measurement.
honest_version: An honest claim shows the rig, the game, repeated runs, and the noise floor — and is willing to report "no measurable change," which is the most common honest answer.

name: The mismatched before/after
pattern: A side-by-side shows low FPS "before" and high FPS "after." Look closer and the two shots are different scenes, different settings, or different spots in the game — the gap is from changing the test, not the tweak.
tell: The two images don't match: a different area, a quality preset, or a menu versus gameplay does the heavy lifting, not the change being sold.
honest_version: An honest comparison holds everything identical except the one change, in the same scene, measured the same way.

name: The subscription trap on local-only work
pattern: A tool charges a recurring fee for things that happen entirely on your own PC and need no ongoing service — toggling settings, clearing temp files, "optimizing." The repeated billing is the business model; the work is one-time and free elsewhere.
tell: You're billed monthly or yearly for changes that live entirely on your machine, with no real service being delivered over time.
honest_version: An honest tool charges once or stays free for local-only work, and never holds an undo button or a basic setting behind a renewal.

name: "Secret settings Microsoft hides from you"
pattern: A video or app frames ordinary, well-documented options as forbidden secrets "they don't want you to know." The conspiracy framing turns boring or useless toggles into must-click revelations.
tell: The pitch leans on secrecy and insider language instead of showing a measured result — if it were a real win, it wouldn't need a conspiracy.
honest_version: An honest tool explains what a setting does in plain language and shows whether it actually helps, secret or not.

name: The bundled-bloat installer
pattern: The installer for one tool quietly tucks in two or three others — a browser toolbar, a different "optimizer," an antivirus trial — with the consent boxes pre-checked. Click through fast and you've installed a small crowd you never wanted.
tell: The setup has extra pre-ticked checkboxes and "recommended" partner offers you have to actively decline on each screen.
honest_version: An honest installer installs the one thing you asked for and bundles nothing you didn't choose.

name: The testimonial wall
pattern: Instead of a measurement, the page is a wall of glowing quotes, five-star ratings, and "trusted by millions." Social proof stands in for evidence the thing actually works, and "feels faster" quotes are exactly what the placebo effect produces.
tell: Lots of feelings, faces, and star ratings — and not a single repeatable before-and-after number anywhere.
honest_version: An honest tool leads with what it measured and how, and treats "feels faster" as a question to test, not proof.

name: Paid one-click "PC optimizers"
pattern: A paid app sells one button that supposedly makes your whole PC — and your games — faster. Inside, it bundles the familiar kit: a registry "clean," a "RAM optimizer," a sweep of service and telemetry toggles, and some automatic process-priority shuffling, then hands it all back as one big improvement you just paid for.
tell: It sells a feeling, never a number — "smoother," "snappier," "up to X% faster," with no before/after you can measure. The same one-click pitch is aimed at every PC no matter its hardware, and the few changes in there that genuinely help are mixed in with placebo and risk so the bundle looks worth the price.
honest_version: Almost everything that actually helps in those suites is a free, built-in Windows setting you can flip yourself and undo in seconds — and several of the rest do nothing, or can cause instability. An honest tool tells you which is which for YOUR hardware, shows the measured effect, and never charges a subscription to toggle a setting Windows already has.
